INTERVENOR THE ESTATE AND TRUST OF JOYCE ANN RUNDBERG’S
INITIAL BRIEF
I.  INTRODUCTION
Intervenor the Estate and Trust of Joyce Ann Rundberg (the “Estate”), by and through its Personal Representative, Brenda Rundberg, owns Tract 2641.1, approximately 88 acres at 100 Rundberg Drive, Jarrell, Williamson County, Texas, in the path of Applicants’ proposed Link F41 of the Bell County East Switch to Big Hill Substation 765-kV Transmission Line Project. Link F41 would cross Tract 2641.1 for approximately 1,835 linear feet, burdening approximately 8.42 additional acres of the property.
The record demonstrates that Link F41 is not the route best supported by the statutory criteria under PURA § 37.056(c) and 16 TAC § 25.101 as applied to Tract 2641.1. The property already carries two pre-existing encumbrances imposed within the prior three years: a 10.36-acre right-of-way taking for the Ronald Reagan (FM 1105) roadway extension that eliminated approximately 80 percent of the property’s primary hayfield, and a perpetual 20-foot Jarrell-Schwertner Water Supply Corporation utility easement. Stacking a third corridor on top of these encumbrances imposes disproportionate cumulative harm on a property whose agricultural productivity has already been severely compromised. Link F41 as currently routed also crosses directly over the property’s back stock tank, the sole water source for 17 head of cattle, passes through confirmed Texas Horned Lizard habitat and two active native harvester ant colonies, and runs in proximity to the Holy Trinity Catholic Church and Cemetery and the Islamic Center of Jarrell. Applicants changed the F41 route between the June 2025 landowner meeting and the filed application without providing notice to the Estate.
The Estate respectfully requests that the Commission deny approval of Link F41 across Tract 2641.1 as currently routed and direct Applicants to conduct a bona fide route alternative analysis that accounts for cumulative impact, threatened species habitat, stock tank impacts, and cultural resources.
In the alternative, if the Commission approves Link F41 in any alignment, the Estate requests binding mitigation conditions addressing threatened-species impacts, water supply protection, cultural resource assessment, and notice and compensation for cumulative severance damages.
II.  PROCEDURAL BACKGROUND
Applicants filed a Joint Application seeking to amend their Certificates of Convenience and Necessity (“CCN”) to construct the Bell County East Switch to Big Hill Substation 765-kV transmission line through Bell, Burnet, Concho, Coryell, Lampasas, Llano, Mason, McCulloch, Menard, Milam, Mills, San Saba, Schleicher, Tom Green, and Williamson Counties. The proceeding was assigned PUC Docket No. 59475 and SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349.
On April 26, 2026, the Estate timely filed its Motion to Intervene and obtained full party status as a landowner whose property is adversely affected by the proposed route. The Estate was represented throughout by M. Bryon Barnhill of the Law Office of M. Bryon Barnhill PLLC, Gatesville, Texas.
The Hearing on the Merits was conducted June 8–12, 2026, at the LCRA Dalchau Service Center in Austin, Texas. Brenda Rundberg appeared and presented sworn testimony concerning the impacts of Link F41 on Tract 2641.1. The evidentiary record closed June 12, 2026. This Initial Brief is filed pursuant to the procedural schedule established by SOAH Order No. 6.
III.  GOVERNING LEGAL STANDARD
PURA Section 37.056(c) requires the Commission to evaluate a CCN amendment application on the basis of the “best interests of the landowners and the public” and to consider specific statutory routing factors. Those factors include: the effect on the environment; the effect on the scenic and aesthetic character of the area; the effect on the value of property; compliance with applicable laws and regulations; the use of existing rights-of-way; and effects on habitable structures. 16 TAC § 25.101 implements these factors and establishes the framework for comparative route analysis.
The burden of proof rests with Applicants to demonstrate that the proposed route is the route best supported by the statutory factors. It is not sufficient for Applicants to show that Link F41 is a permissible route; they must demonstrate it is the best route under the statutory criteria. Where the record reveals that a proposed route imposes disproportionate and cumulative harm on an already-burdened property, without adequate alternatives analysis, the Commission should deny approval or impose binding conditions.
IV.  LINK F41 IS NOT THE ROUTE BEST SUPPORTED BY THE STATUTORY FACTORS
A.  Cumulative Impact: Three Encumbrances Render the Remainder Potentially Non-Viable
Tract 2641.1 is an approximately 88-acre active agricultural property supporting 17 head of cattle, hay production, dove, turkey, and deer hunting, and a natural honeybee hive. Before Link F41, the property already carries two significant encumbrances imposed within approximately the prior three years: (1) a 10.36-acre right-of-way taking for the Ronald Reagan (FM 1105) roadway extension recorded December 5, 2025, which eliminated approximately 80 percent of the property’s hayfield, the primary feed source for the cattle herd; and (2) a perpetual 20-foot Jarrell-Schwertner Water Supply Corporation utility easement executed January 26, 2023. These two encumbrances have already materially reduced the productive acreage of Tract 2641.1 and impaired the cattle operation.
The proposed Link F41 corridor would burden an additional 8.42 acres across the property’s midsection for its full 1,835-foot width, dividing the tract into functionally disconnected segments and imposing a third belt of restricted-use land. The cumulative result is a property whose two principal agricultural resources, the hayfield and the back stock tank, are either eliminated or directly threatened. Applicants’ routing analysis does not appear to account for the Ronald Reagan taking or the Schwertner easement in evaluating the cumulative compatibility impact on Tract 2641.1. An analysis that ignores two pre-existing encumbrances cannot fairly determine whether F41 is the best route under the statutory criteria as applied to this property.
B.  Stock Tank Destruction and Water Supply
The updated Link F41 centerline, as reflected in the May 11, 2026 LCRA route map, crosses directly over the back stock tank on Tract 2641.1, the critical water source for the cattle operation. Tower placement and construction activity in proximity to the tank threaten contamination, structural disruption, and destruction of the riparian and aquatic habitat the tank supports. Cattle without reliable water cannot be safely maintained on the property. If the stock tank is compromised, the Estate would be required to develop alternative water infrastructure at significant cost. Applicants have not identified the stock tank crossing as a design constraint or offered to avoid or offset this impact.
Four water wells are located on Tract 2641.1. Each is at risk from construction vibration, equipment traffic, and permanent electromagnetic field exposure from the 765-kV conductor. Applicants have not addressed water well risk in their environmental or engineering filings.
C.  Failure to Parallel Existing Rights-of-Way
Link F41 cuts a new corridor across Tract 2641.1. It does not follow any existing transmission line right-of-way, roadway corridor, or compatible land-use buffer across the property. The statutory preference for routing along existing ROW and compatible corridors is a fundamental criterion under PURA § 37.056(c) and 16 TAC § 25.101, precisely because parallelism minimizes new encumbrances on previously undisturbed agricultural land. Applicants have not demonstrated that the Ronald Reagan right-of-way corridor adjacent to Tract 2641.1 was meaningfully evaluated as a parallelism option, or that any comparable parallelism alternative was assessed and found inferior.
D.  Environmental Constraints: Texas Horned Lizard and Wildlife Habitat
The Texas Horned Lizard (Phrynosoma cornutum) is listed as a Threatened species under Texas law. Tex. Parks & Wildlife Code § 67.004; 31 Tex. Admin. Code § 65.175. Brenda Rundberg’s sworn testimony confirms the presence of the Texas Horned Lizard on Tract 2641.1 within the direct path of the Link F41 centerline. The F41 centerline also passes directly through the locations of two active native harvester ant (Pogonomyrmex spp.) colonies. The native harvester ant is the primary food source of the Texas Horned Lizard; destruction of these colonies eliminates the food base that sustains the lizard population on the property. Applicants’ environmental resource assessment does not reflect a site-specific survey of Tract 2641.1 for Texas Horned Lizard presence or native harvester ant colonies.
The F41 corridor also crosses habitat supporting diverse resident and migratory wildlife, including waterfowl dependent on the stock tanks, upland game, and raptors. The stock tank crossing in particular represents a direct threat to aquatic and riparian habitat that serves as a critical wildlife refuge on this agricultural landscape.
E.  Effect on Historical and Cultural Sites
The proposed Link F41 route passes in close proximity to two historically and culturally significant community institutions. The Holy Trinity Catholic Church and Cemetery (8626 FM 1105), a historic Roman Catholic church and cemetery founded by Czech immigrant settlers in the nineteenth century, is located immediately adjacent to the F41 route corridor. The Islamic Center of Jarrell (9401 FM 1105) is located directly across FM 1105 from the proposed route. Neither institution was addressed in Applicants’ cultural resource assessment with respect to the specific impacts of Link F41. An unpreserved historic timber road running along the south and southwest borders of Tract 2641.1 is also not reflected on any survey or routing map produced by Applicants in this proceeding.
F.  Health, Safety, and Residential Proximity
The proposed Link F41 line would place a 765-kV transmission conductor in close proximity to the Rundberg family residence and working barns. Peer-reviewed scientific research has documented associations between long-term residential exposure to electromagnetic fields generated by high-voltage transmission lines and adverse health outcomes. Applicants have not produced a health impact assessment specific to the residential exposure that would result from siting a 765-kV line at the proximity established by the F41 route as filed. The burden of demonstrating consistency with public health and safety rests with the Applicants. In addition, scientific literature documents concerns regarding the effects of high-voltage electromagnetic fields on livestock, including behavioral disruption, reduced weight gain, and reproductive irregularities. Applicants have not addressed livestock health or safety in their filings.
G.  Effect on Agricultural Use, Property Values, and Community Character
Tract 2641.1 is an active agricultural property carrying an agricultural tax exemption. The Link F41 corridor would bisect the remaining grazing field, divide the tract into disconnected segments, impose permanent tower structures incompatible with free-range cattle operations, and eliminate unrestricted field access across the proposed easement strip. The cumulative effect of three encumbrances within approximately a two-to-three-year window on a single agricultural property is severe.
Tract 2641.1 lies in a Williamson County market experiencing active residential and commercial development pressure. Texas and national real estate research consistently documents that high-voltage transmission lines devalue adjacent and encumbered properties through visual impact, noise from corona discharge, use restrictions within the easement corridor, and buyer hesitation driven by perceived health risks. A buyer evaluating Tract 2641.1 after F41 is constructed would confront a tract burdened by three separate encumbrances imposed within approximately two to three years. These devaluation effects are squarely within the factors the Commission is required to weigh under PURA § 37.056(c).
V.  APPLICANTS’ ENGINEERING ANALYSIS IS DEFICIENT
As established in prior SOAH proceedings and in testimony in this proceeding, no qualified, independent engineering study of the Basin Reliability Plan at certified 765-kV standards has been confirmed. Applicants’ engineers appear to have applied 345-kV design standards to a 765-kV project. The choice of voltage level directly determines the required easement width, tower height, conductor clearance distances, and the radius of significant electromagnetic field exposure. A routing analysis premised on the wrong design standard may systematically understate the land burden, property impacts, and health and safety implications for every affected landowner. The Estate respectfully urges the ALJs to condition any CCN approval on submission of a qualified, independent engineering validation of the Basin Reliability Plan at certified 765-kV standards.
Separately, Applicants changed the F41 route between the June 2025 landowner meeting and the filed application without providing notice to the Estate. The changed route, now crossing directly over the back stock tank and through confirmed threatened-species habitat, was more burdensome than the alignment presented to landowners in June 2025. The Estate first learned of the changed alignment through review of the application documents. This procedural failure deprived the Estate of a meaningful opportunity to respond to the changed routing prior to the proceeding’s initial deadlines and warrants heightened scrutiny of the F41 routing determination.
VI.  SUMMARY: STATUTORY FACTOR COMPARISON

VII.  ALTERNATIVE RELIEF: BINDING MITIGATION CONDITIONS
In the event the Commission approves Link F41 across Tract 2641.1 in any alignment, the Estate requests the following binding mitigation conditions be imposed on Applicants as a condition of the CCN amendment:
(1) A TPWD-coordinated, site-specific biological survey for Texas Horned Lizard and native harvester ant colonies within the Link F41 corridor on Tract 2641.1, conducted prior to any construction activity, with avoidance, minimization, and mitigation measures required for any confirmed impacts, and any required TPWD permits obtained before ground disturbance commences;
(2) Pre-construction survey and post-construction monitoring of each of the four water wells on Tract 2641.1 at Applicants’ sole expense, with replacement or repair at Applicants’ expense if any well is damaged or impaired by construction activity or by the permanent infrastructure;
(3) Construction measures specifically protective of the back stock tank, including tower placement and access road routing that avoids direct crossing of or proximity to the tank, or full replacement of the tank at Applicants’ expense if avoidance is not achieved;
(4) A qualified cultural resource survey specifically addressing the unpreserved historic timber road along the south and southwest borders of Tract 2641.1 and the proximity of the Holy Trinity Catholic Church and Cemetery, conducted prior to ground disturbance, with any required mitigation measures;
(5) Engineering validation of all design parameters at certified 765-kV standards, submitted to the Commission prior to the issuance of any construction permit;
(6) Written re-engagement with Brenda Rundberg, as Personal Representative of the Estate, providing specific, plain-language notice of the final approved alignment, no fewer than 30 days prior to commencement of any construction activity on Tract 2641.1;
(7) Restoration of all disturbed agricultural land on Tract 2641.1 to pre-construction condition at Applicants’ sole expense upon completion of construction;
(8) A comprehensive land damage assessment accounting for the cumulative impact of the Ronald Reagan taking, the Schwertner easement, and the F41 easement on the market value of the remainder of Tract 2641.1, to be submitted to the Commission and made part of the administrative record.
VIII.  PRESERVATION OF THE RECORD ON DAMAGES
The Estate recognizes that compensation for the taking of an easement is determined in a subsequent condemnation proceeding in state district court, not by the Commission in this docket. Nevertheless, the Estate requests that the ALJs and the Commission preserve the administrative record in this docket for use in any condemnation proceeding involving Tract 2641.1, including all testimony, exhibits, and findings addressing the impacts of Link F41 on the property.
The record in this docket documents the following categories of compensable injury to Tract 2641.1:
(1) Easement strip value: The per-acre or per-linear-foot value of the 765-kV transmission easement across the 1,835 linear feet and approximately 8.42 acres of Tract 2641.1, to be established by appraisal under Texas condemnation law;
(2) Remainder damages, cumulative encumbrance: The diminution in value of the remainder caused by the combined effect of the Ronald Reagan right-of-way taking, the Schwertner utility easement, and the F41 easement, including loss of agricultural cohesion and development potential in a Williamson County market;
(3) Remainder damages, stock tank loss: Destruction or impairment of the back stock tank, including cost of replacement and loss of the agricultural water supply and wildlife habitat value it supports;
(4) Remainder damages, water wells: Risk to and potential loss of any of the four domestic and agricultural water wells, including testing, remediation, and replacement costs;
(5) Remainder damages, agricultural use impairment: Disruption of the cattle operation, loss of unrestricted field access across the proposed easement strip, and impairment of the agricultural tax exemption;
(6) Remainder damages, threatened species mitigation costs: Any costs imposed on the Estate as a result of threatened species impacts attributable to the F41 construction and operation;
(7) Remainder damages, cultural resource impairment: Any costs or diminution in value attributable to impacts on the historic timber road or the proximity of the route to Holy Trinity Catholic Church and Cemetery.
These categories are supported by the testimony of Brenda Rundberg and by the exhibits admitted into the record in this docket.
IX.  PRAYER FOR RELIEF
For all the foregoing reasons, Intervenor the Estate and Trust of Joyce Ann Rundberg, by and through its Personal Representative, Brenda Rundberg, respectfully requests that the Commission:
(1) DENY Applicants’ request to amend their CCNs to construct the Bell County East Switch to Big Hill Substation 765-kV Transmission Line along Link F41 across Tract 2641.1 in the currently filed alignment, and DIRECT Applicants to conduct a bona fide route alternative analysis for F41 that accounts for cumulative impact, confirmed Texas Horned Lizard habitat and native harvester ant colony locations, the back stock tank crossing, Holy Trinity Catholic Church and Cemetery proximity, and the unpreserved historic timber road along the southern border of Tract 2641.1;
(2) In the alternative, IMPOSE the binding mitigation conditions set forth in Section VII of this Brief as a condition of any CCN amendment approving Link F41 across Tract 2641.1 in any alignment;
(3) PRESERVE for the administrative record all testimony and exhibits concerning damages to Tract 2641.1, including the cumulative encumbrance evidence, stock tank and water well risk documentation, threatened species testimony, and cultural resource and property value evidence presented in this proceeding;
(4) FIND that Applicants’ failure to provide notice of the route change between the June 2025 landowner meeting alignment and the filed application is a procedural irregularity warranting heightened scrutiny of the F41 routing determination;
(5) FIND that Applicants’ engineering analysis cannot be confirmed to satisfy 765-kV design standards and require independent engineering validation as a condition of any CCN amendment;
(6) GRANT the Estate such other and further relief to which it may be justly entitled.

Respectfully submitted,

and the filed application without providing notice to the Estate. The changed route, now crossing
directly over the back stock tank and through confirmed threatened-species habitat, was more
burdensome than the alignment presented to landowners in June 2025. The Estate first learned of
the changed alignment through review of the application documents. This procedural failure
deprived the Estate of a meaningful opportunity to respond to the changed routing prior to the
proceeding's initial deadlines and warrants heightened scrutiny ofthe F41 routing determination.

          VII. ALTERNATIVE RELIEF: BINDING MITIGATION CONDITIONS
        In the event the Commission approves Link F41 across Tract 2641.1 in any alignment,
the Estate requests the following binding mitigation conditions be imposed on Applicants as a
condition ofthe CCN amendment:
        (1) A TPWD-coordinated, site-specific biological survey for Texas Horned Lizard and
native harvester ant colonies within the Link F41 corridor on Tract 2641.1, conducted prior to
any construction activity, with avoidance, minimization, and mitigation measures required for
any confirmed impacts, and any required TPWD permits obtained before ground disturbance
commences;
       (2) Pre-construction survey and post-construction monitoring of each of the four water
wells on Tract 2641.1 at Applicants' sole expense, with replacement or repair at Applicants'
expense if any well is damaged or impaired by construction activity or by the permanent
infrastructure;
       (3) Construction measures specifically protective of the back stock tank, including tower
placement and access road routing that avoids direct crossing of or proximity to the tank, or full
replacement of the tank at Applicants' expense if avoidance is not achieved;
        (4) A qualified cultural resource survey specifically addressing the unpreserved historic
timber road along the south and southwest borders of Tract 2641.1 and the proximity ofthe Holy
Trinity Catholic Church and Cemetery, conducted prior to ground disturbance, with any required
mitigation measures;
       (5) Engineering validation of all design parameters at certified 765-kV standards,
submitted to the Commission prior to the issuance of any construction permit;
        (6) Written re-engagement with Brenda Rundberg, as Personal Representative of the
Estate, providing specific, plain-language notice of the final approved alignment, no fewer than
30 days prior to commencement of any construction activity on Tract 2641.1;
        (7) Restoration of all disturbed agricultural land on Tract 2641.1 to pre-construction
condition at Applicants' sole expense upon completion of construction;
       (8) A comprehensive land damage assessment accounting for the cumulative impact of
the Ronald Reagan taking, the Schwertner easement, and the F41 easement on the market value
ofthe remainder of Tract 2641.1, to be submitted to the Commission and made part ofthe
administrative record.

                VIII. PRESERVATION OF THE RECORD ON DAMAGES
       The Estate recognizes that compensation for the taking of an easement is determined in a
subsequent condemnation proceeding in state district court, not by the Commission in this
docket. Nevertheless, the Estate requests that the ALJs and the Commission preserve the
 administrative record in this docket for use in any condemnation proceeding involving Tract
2641.1, including all testimony, exhibits, and findings addressing the impacts of Link F41 on the
property.
       The record in this docket documents the following categories of compensable injury to
Tract 2641.1:
        (1) Easement strip value: The per-acre or per-linear-foot value of the 765-kV
transmission easement across the 1,835 linear feet and approximately 8.42 acres of Tract 2641.1,
to be established by appraisal under Texas condemnation law;
       (2) Remainder damages, cumulative encumbrance: The diminution in value of the
remainder caused by the combined effect of the Ronald Reagan right-of-way taking, the
Schwertner utility easement, and the F41 easement, including loss of agricultural cohesion and
development potential in a Williamson County market;
       (3) Remainder damages, stock tank loss: Destruction or impairment of the back stock
tank, including cost of replacement and loss of the agricultural water supply and wildlife habitat
value it supports;
       (4) Remainder damages, water wells: Risk to and potential loss of any ofthe four
domestic and agricultural water wells, including testing, remediation, and replacement costs;
       (5) Remainder damages, agricultural use impairment: Disruption ofthe cattle operation,
loss ofunrestricted field access across the proposed easement strip, and impairment ofthe
agricultural tax exemption;
        (6) Remainder damages, threatened species mitigation costs: Any costs imposed on the
Estate as a result ofthreatened species impacts attributable to the F41 construction and operation;
         (7) Remainder damages, cultural resource impairment: Any costs or diminution in value
attributable to impacts on the historic timber road or the proximity of the route to Holy Trinity
Catholic Church and Cemetery.
       These categories are supported by the testimony of Brenda Rundberg and by the exhibits
admitted into the record in this docket.
